To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the intensity of vection induced by visual yaw rotation around the vertical body axis is related to the magnitude of the optokinetic after-nystagmus (the discharge of the velocity store mechanism) which is in turn a factor in motion-sickness.
vection intensity was related to VSM charging, and that VSM activity was related to motion sickness.

1) vection intensity is a determinant factor in VIMS; 2) the intensity of the vection correlates with the charging of the velocity storage system; 3) the charging of the central integrative network is a factor in VIMS.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how visual motion stimuli can cause motion sickness.
the question of how the visual system is involved in the generation and control of motion sickness.
the question of how visual motion stimuli are processed by the central nervous system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
more vection means more VSM activity which means more VIMS.
the stronger the vection the stronger the motion sickness, and that this effect is mediated by the VSM.
more vection means more OKAN, and thus more VSM activity and eventually more VIMS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
vection and motion sickness are related, but not necessarily through a common mechanism.
VSM activity is a factor in VIMS, but that it does not fully explain the intensity of VIMS.
VIMS is a consequence of the VSM being overcharged, which is caused by strong vection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the VSM is a key player in the development of VIMS.
the intensity of vection is related to the activity of the velocity storage network.
visual stimuli that elicit a strong sense of self-motion are more likely to induce motion sickness than those inducing a weak sense of self motion.
